name: Acne
definition: Acne is a common skin condition in which spots, from a few small ones to deep painful lumps, appear mostly on the face, chest and back.
overview: Acne happens when hair follicles in the skin become clogged with oil and dead skin cells, and bacteria then multiply in them. Changes in hormones are a major factor, and acne tends to run in families. It can range from mild, with a few spots, to severe, with deep and painful lumps under the skin. It can also affect mental health. Treatment is available from pharmacists and GPs, and some people are referred to a skin specialist.
causes: Hair follicles become clogged with oil and dead skin cells, and bacteria can then multiply in them.
Hormone changes are a major factor.
Oil glands can be sensitive to hormones even when hormone levels are normal, which leads to extra oil.
Acne also tends to run in families.
Cleaning the skin does not remove the blockage, and there is no evidence that poor hygiene or sexual activity cause acne.
riskFactors: Hormonal conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome.
Some medicines, including some contraceptives, high-dose steroids and anabolic steroids.
Greasy skin or hair products, and picking at the skin.
signs: Open (black) and closed (white) comedones, which are blackheads and whiteheads.
Nodules and cysts in more severe acne.
Lesions mainly on the face, neck, upper back and chest.
Scarring, which clinicians note, including its type.
complications: Permanent scarring, especially if spots are squeezed or picked.
Persistent changes in skin colour after spots heal.
Psychological distress and mental health problems, which can occur with acne of any severity.
Signs of skin infection in affected spots.
diagnosis: Acne is assessed from the skin itself, including the number, type and distribution of the lesions. Clinicians also note whether scarring is present and what type it is. The person's own views of how acne affects them are taken into account.
treatment: For a few blackheads, whiteheads and spots, a pharmacist can advise on gels or creams that can be bought without a prescription. These often contain benzoyl peroxide. Prescription treatments include topical retinoids, topical antibiotics, azelaic acid and antibiotic tablets. The combined contraceptive pill is another option for women. Antibiotic tablets are generally used alongside topical treatments for severe acne. Isotretinoin is a capsule treatment for severe acne that has not responded to other treatments, and the NHS says it can only be prescribed by a specialist doctor.
prevention: The NHS describes some everyday skin care steps for people with acne. The NHS describes washing with a gentle cleanser, using non-comedogenic products and removing make-up at night. It advises against squeezing spots, because this can cause permanent scarring.
seekCare: A pharmacist is the usual first contact for a few blackheads, whiteheads and spots. A GP appointment is advised if self-treatment is not helping, if there are many spots, deep or painful spots, or spots that scar. A GP appointment is also advised if there are signs of skin infection, or if acne is affecting mental health. A GP can refer a person to a skin specialist (dermatologist). If low mood becomes serious, NHS 111 can help, and Samaritans are free on 116 123 at any time. Anyone in immediate danger should call 999.

references.title: British Association of Dermatologists: Acne patient information leaflet

sections.heading: What does acne look like?
sections.body:
Acne can range from mild, with a few spots, to severe, with deep and painful lumps under the skin. It most often appears on the face, then the back, then the chest. The NHS lists six main types of spot: blackheads, whiteheads, papules, pustules, nodules and cysts. Blackheads are black or yellowish and are dark because of pigment in the lining of the follicle, not because of dirt. Whiteheads are similar but firmer, and they do not empty when squeezed.

Papules are small, tender red bumps, and pustules are papules with a white tip filled with pus. Nodules are large, hard and often painful lumps under the skin. Cysts are the most severe type, being large lumps filled with pus, and they carry the greatest risk of permanent scarring. Clinicians describe severity along a continuum, using the distribution, number and type of lesions and the person's own views.

sections.heading: What causes acne?
sections.body:
Acne starts when hair follicles become clogged with oil and dead skin cells, and bacteria then multiply in the blocked follicles. Hormone changes are a major factor, and acne also tends to run in families. The BAD leaflet says the oil glands can be sensitive to hormones even when hormone levels are normal. It also lists hormonal causes such as polycystic ovary syndrome, some contraceptives, high-dose steroids and anabolic steroids.

Oily skincare products, greasy hair products and picking at the skin can make acne worse. The NHS says that cleaning the skin does not remove the blockage in the follicles. It also says there is no evidence that poor hygiene or sexual activity cause acne. On diet, the BAD leaflet says there is not enough evidence to support particular diets for treating acne, though a healthy, balanced diet is advisable.

sections.heading: How does skin care help with acne?
sections.body:
The NHS self-care advice is to wash with a gentle cleanser twice a day, use non-comedogenic products and remove make-up at night. The NHS advises against squeezing spots or trying to clear blackheads, because this can cause permanent scarring. NICE gives similar advice, noting that persistent picking or scratching of lesions can increase the risk of scarring.

For a few blackheads, whiteheads and spots, a pharmacist should be able to advise on gels or creams that can be bought over the counter. Products with benzoyl peroxide or salicylic acid are options. The BAD leaflet describes benzoyl peroxide, azelaic acid and nicotinamide as first-step options that can take a few months to work.

sections.heading: How is acne treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says a GP can offer prescription treatments if pharmacy products have not worked or acne is more severe. These include topical retinoids, topical antibiotics, azelaic acid and antibiotic tablets, and for women the combined contraceptive pill. Antibiotic tablets are generally used alongside topical treatments for severe acne. NICE describes treatment as typically offered as a course that is reviewed after about three months, taking account of severity and the person's preferences.

Many of these treatments can take a couple of months or more before they start to work. Isotretinoin is a treatment for severe acne that comes as capsules. The NHS says it is only considered for severe acne that has not responded to other treatments. Because of the risk of side effects, the NHS says isotretinoin can only be prescribed by a specialist doctor. Dry skin and lips are common side effects, and mood is monitored during treatment. The BAD leaflet notes that isotretinoin also has pregnancy restrictions.

sections.heading: When should someone see a doctor about acne?
sections.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP if self-treatment is not helping, if there are many spots, or if spots are deep, painful or leave scars. A GP appointment is also advised if there are signs of skin infection or if acne is affecting mental health. A GP can refer a person to a dermatologist, a doctor who specialises in skin. NICE lists reasons for referral including acne that has not responded to two completed courses of treatment, acne leading to scarring, and persistent changes in skin colour.

NICE also says acne of any severity can cause psychological distress and mental health problems. Treatment therefore aims to protect against both physical scarring and psychological harm. In an emergency, such as someone in immediate danger, call 999.

sections.heading: What is the outlook for acne?
sections.body: The BAD leaflet says acne usually fades by the early to mid-twenties, though it can last longer or start later in adult life. It says there is currently no cure, but effective treatment can prevent new spots and reduce scarring. The NHS notes that acne can take several months to improve with treatment. The NHS says a GP can refer people to a dermatologist if acne is severe or prescription medicines are not working. Reasons for referral include painful nodules, scarring or a risk of scarring, or acne that is making a person feel very low or anxious. NICE says scar management is usually considered after the skin has finished remodelling, which can take up to about a year after the acne has cleared.

faqs.q: Is acne caused by dirt or poor hygiene?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no evidence that poor hygiene or sexual activity cause acne. It also says cleaning the skin does not remove the blockage that forms in the hair follicles. Blackheads are dark because of pigment in the follicle lining, not because of dirt.

The NHS advises against squeezing spots or trying to clear blackheads, because this can cause permanent scarring. NICE also says persistent picking or scratching of lesions can increase the risk of scarring. For a few spots, the NHS says a pharmacist can advise on gels or creams that can be bought over the counter.

The BAD leaflet says there is currently no cure for acne. It adds that effective treatment can prevent new spots and reduce scarring, and that acne usually fades by the early to mid-twenties. It can last longer or start later in adult life.

faqs.q: Does diet cause or treat acne?
faqs.a: The BAD leaflet says there is not enough evidence to back specific diets for treating acne. It says a healthy, balanced diet is advisable. Hormone changes, extra oil in the skin and blocked follicles are the main causes the NHS and BAD describe.

The NHS describes isotretinoin as a capsule treatment for severe acne that has not responded to other treatments. Because of the risk of side effects, the NHS says it can only be prescribed by a specialist doctor. Dry skin and lips are common side effects, and mood is monitored during treatment.

Yes, the NHS says acne can affect mental health. NICE says acne of any severity can cause psychological distress. The NHS advises seeing a GP if acne is affecting mental health. NICE says treatment aims to protect against both physical scarring and psychological harm. A GP can refer a person to a dermatologist.
